summary: Looks at how the RFC Editor, as archivist of the RFC Series, should preserve RFCs. It gives guidance on when and how to preserve them, describes tools needed to view or re-create them, and points out gaps in current process.

plainLanguage.summary: Old books need to be kept safe so people can still read them years from now. This explains how the library of RFCs should be looked after.

questions: how should rfcs be preserved for the future
what formats should rfcs be archived in
subtitle: How to preserve RFCs as digital technology changes.

tldr.problem: The RFC Series is getting more complex with new formats and metadata, making it harder to preserve for future generations using the old simple archive process.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC Editor adopts a digital preservation strategy that balances archival best practices with cost and complexity, choosing which file formats and computing environments to preserve long-term.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8153 gives the RFC Editor and community a framework for deciding how to preserve RFCs so they remain readable and accessible decades or centuries into the future.

today: RFC 8153 is an Informational RFC from the Internet Architecture Board providing guidance on RFC Series preservation. It has not been obsoleted and remains the primary document describing how the RFC Editor should archive RFCs as formats and technology evolve.

sections.title: The Challenge of Preserving RFCs
sections.content:
The RFC Series is both published and archived by the RFC Editor. The tension lies between two roles: as a publisher, the RFC Editor wants to use modern features like hyperlinks, rich metadata, and multiple file formats to serve today's readers; as an archivist, it must preserve documents so they can be read and understood far into the future, even as technology changes. These goals conflict.

For decades, this was simple: RFCs were plain ASCII text, a format so basic that it is unlikely to become unreadable. Today, RFCs are produced in XML with multiple publication formats including HTML and PDF, each with richer features but also more fragility. This RFC describes how to navigate this tension, drawing on the ISO Open Archival Information System (OAIS) reference model used by digital archives worldwide.
sections.plainLanguage: RFCs need to be both easy to read now and safe to read in 100 years. Old plain text files never break, but new fancy formats might not work when technology changes.

sections.title: Preservation Concepts and Process
sections.content:
The document defines two key preservation concepts. Bitstream preservation means keeping the raw data (the zeros and ones of the files) safe and unchanged, typically through disk backups and regular maintenance. Content preservation means ensuring the data can still be read and understood by humans or tools in the future, even if the original software is gone.

The preservation process follows a life cycle: Acquisition happens when an Internet-Draft is approved for publication. Ingestion is when the RFC is published and assigned unique metadata like its RFC number, ISSN, and Digital Object Identifier (DOI). The RFC Editor then records extensive metadata in a central registry, including author, title, publication date, and references. Bitstream preservation is maintained through standard IT practices like disk mirroring and off-site backups. For content preservation, all RFCs since January 2010 have been printed on paper as a backup, though the document argues this is no longer sufficient for complex new formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping the computer files safe is one job. Making sure you can actually open and read them in the future is a harder job. Both need to happen.

sections.title: Three Archival Options
sections.content:
The document describes three possible approaches, ranked by complexity and cost. The simplest is best-effort data retention, which relies on standard IT backup practices: disk mirroring, off-site storage, and regular restoration tests. This has worked well for plain text and ASCII for decades, but it is likely insufficient for complex formats like XML and PDF that may become unreadable in 50 to 100 years as software evolves.

The second approach is single-format archival, where one stable file format is chosen as the archival standard. PDF/A-3, an ISO-standardized archival format for electronic documents, was designed for long-term preservation and can embed the source XML inside it. This avoids the need to preserve entire software environments, but relies on PDF/A-3 remaining readable in the distant future—a gamble the document acknowledges.

The third and most thorough approach is holistic environment preservation, archiving not just the files but every operating system, software version, browser, and PDF reader needed to view them. This is best practice from an archivist's perspective but is expensive and becomes more costly as technology accumulates over decades. The document notes this approach may require resources beyond what the RFC Editor can sustain.
sections.plainLanguage: Option 1: Hope the files stay readable (risky). Option 2: Pick one format that was designed to last (better). Option 3: Keep copies of all the old software too (expensive but safest).

sections.title: Recommended Preservation Strategy
sections.content:
The document recommends a middle path that balances best practice with cost. Preservation should focus on archiving the canonical XML files and PDF/A-3 files, with the PDF/A-3 file embedding the XML inside it for future validation. Multiple major versions of the xml2rfc tool used to create RFCs, plus its documentation, should be retained. At least two PDF reader applications should be archived to ensure future access. All other formats and the general computing environment should follow best-effort data retention.

The RFC recommends discontinuing the practice of printing every RFC to paper upon publication, arguing that digital storage and mirrored copies provide more reliable protection against catastrophic loss. Instead, the RFC Editor should partner with specialized digital preservation organizations around the world to mirror and ingest RFC collections. These partners should ingest the entire context of each RFC: the canonical file, all metadata, digital signatures, and the original submitted Internet-Draft.

Finally, preservation efforts should be validated through a biennial audit confirming that all archived content and metadata can still be read with current tools, following the audit guidelines from the ISO standard for trustworthy digital repositories.
sections.plainLanguage: Save the XML and the PDF files. Keep old versions of the tool that reads them. Partner with other archives to keep multiple copies. Check every two years that everything still works.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The document assumes that the RFC Editor itself is a trusted, secure source and that the publication process for RFCs is secure. With that foundation, the preservation activities discussed—storing backups, maintaining metadata, and archiving tools—do not create new security risks to the Internet itself. However, archives must protect against unauthorized changes to stored RFCs or metadata, which is why digital signatures and integrity checks are important.
sections.plainLanguage: If we trust the RFC Editor, then storing old RFCs safely does not make the Internet less secure.
